column1: # Jāmiʿ al-ʿUlūm wa-l-Ḥikam — Hadith 32: “There is to be no harm and no returning of harm”

column2: From Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī (may Allah be pleased with him): The Prophet ﷺ said: “There is to be no harm and no returning of harm.” A good (ḥasan) hadith, reported by Ibn Mājah, al-Dāraquṭnī and others with a connected chain (musnad).
Mālik reported it in the Muwaṭṭaʾ from ʿAmr ibn Yaḥyā, from his father, from the Prophet ﷺ, in mursal form, leaving out Abū Saʿīd. It has routes of transmission that strengthen one another.
The hadith of Abū Saʿīd was not recorded by Ibn Mājah. It was recorded only by al-Dāraquṭnī, al-Ḥākim and al-Bayhaqī, through the narration of ʿUthmān ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿUthmān ibn Rabīʿah:
al-Darāwardī told us, from ʿAmr ibn Yaḥyā al-Māzinī, from his father, from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, from the Prophet ﷺ,

who said: “There is to be no harm and no returning of harm. Whoever harms, Allah will harm him; and whoever causes hardship, Allah will bring hardship upon him.” Al-Ḥākim said: Its chain is authentic by the criterion of Muslim.
Al-Bayhaqī said: ʿUthmān alone narrated it from al-Darāwardī. Mālik recorded it in the Muwaṭṭaʾ from ʿAmr ibn Yaḥyā, from his father, in mursal form.

Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said: The reports from Mālik do not differ over this hadith being mursal. He said: Nor is it narrated with a connected chain by any authentic route. He then recorded it through the narration of ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Muʿādh al-Naṣībī,

from al-Darāwardī, with a connected chain. Imam Aḥmad used to regard as weak what al-Darāwardī narrated from memory, and paid no heed to it; and there is no doubt that Mālik's version takes precedence over his.
The ḥāfiẓ Khālid ibn Saʿd al-Andalusī said: The hadith “There is to be no harm and no returning of harm” is not authentic with a connected chain.
As for Ibn Mājah, he recorded it through the narration of Fuḍayl ibn Sulaymān: Mūsā ibn ʿUqbah told us: Isḥāq ibn Yaḥyā ibn al-Walīd told me, from ʿUbādah ibn al-Ṣāmit,

that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ decreed that there is to be no harm and no returning of harm. This belongs to a written collection (ṣaḥīfah) narrated with this chain, and it is broken, taken from a book;
so said Ibn al-Madīnī, Abū Zurʿah and others. It is said that Isḥāq ibn Yaḥyā is Ibn Ṭalḥah, who is weak and did not hear from ʿUbādah;

so said Abū Zurʿah, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, and al-Dāraquṭnī in one place. It is also said that he is Isḥāq ibn Yaḥyā ibn al-Walīd ibn ʿUbādah, who likewise did not hear from ʿUbādah; al-Dāraquṭnī said this too.

Ibn ʿAdī mentioned him in his book al-Ḍuʿafāʾ and said: Most of his hadiths are not well preserved. It is also said that Mūsā ibn ʿUqbah did not hear from him, but narrated these hadiths from Abū ʿAyyāsh al-Asadī, from him; and Abū ʿAyyāsh is unknown.

Ibn Mājah also recorded it by another route, through the narration of Jābir al-Juʿfī, from ʿIkrimah, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “There is to be no harm and no returning of harm.”

Most scholars regard Jābir al-Juʿfī as weak. Al-Dāraquṭnī recorded it through the narration of Ibrāhīm ibn Ismāʿīl, from Dāwūd ibn al-Ḥuṣayn, from ʿIkrimah; a number of scholars regard Ibrāhīm as weak, and Dāwūd's narrations from ʿIkrimah are objectionable (manākīr).
Al-Dāraquṭnī recorded, from the hadith of al-Wāqidī: Khārijah ibn ʿAbdullāh ibn Sulaymān ibn Zayd ibn Thābit told us, from Abū al-Rijāl, from ʿAmrah, from ʿĀʾishah, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said:
“There is to be no harm and no returning of harm.” Al-Wāqidī is abandoned (matrūk), and there is disagreement over whether his shaykh is weak.
Al-Ṭabarānī also recorded it by two weak routes, from al-Qāsim, from ʿĀʾishah.

Al-Ṭabarānī also recorded, through the narration of Muḥammad ibn Salamah, from Ibn Isḥāq, from Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā ibn Ḥabbān, from his paternal uncle Wāsiʿ ibn Ḥabbān, from Jābir, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said:

“There is to be no harm and no returning of harm in Islam.” This chain is passable, and the hadith is unusual (gharīb). Abū Dāwūd, however, recorded it in his Marāsīl through the narration of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Maghrāʾ,
from Ibn Isḥāq, from Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā ibn Ḥabbān, from his paternal uncle Wāsiʿ, in mursal form; and that is more correct.
Al-Dāraquṭnī recorded, through the narration of Abū Bakr ibn ʿAyyāsh, who said: I think it was from Ibn ʿAṭāʾ, from his father, from Abū Hurayrah, that the Prophet ﷺ said:
“There is to be no harm and no harming (ḍarūrah), and let none of you prevent his neighbour from placing his timber on his wall.” There is doubt in this chain. Ibn ʿAṭāʾ is Yaʿqūb, and he is weak.

Kathīr ibn ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr ibn ʿAwf al-Muzanī narrated from his father, from his grandfather, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: “There is to be no harm and no returning of harm.” Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said: Its chain is not authentic.

I say: al-Tirmidhī grades the hadith of this Kathīr authentic, and al-Bukhārī says of one of his hadiths: It is the most authentic hadith on the subject. Ibrāhīm ibn al-Mundhir al-Ḥizāmī graded his hadith good, saying:

It is better than the mursal reports of Ibn al-Musayyab. Ibn Abī ʿĀṣim likewise graded it good. Others abandoned his hadith, among them Imam Aḥmad and others. This, then, is what we have at hand of the routes of the hadiths on this subject.

The Shaykh (may Allah have mercy on him) mentioned that some of its routes strengthen others, and it is as he said. Al-Bayhaqī said of some of the hadiths of Kathīr ibn ʿAbdullāh al-Muzanī: When they are joined to other chains that contain weakness, they become strong.

Al-Shāfiʿī said of the mursal hadith: If it is narrated with a connected chain by another route, or if it is narrated in mursal form by someone who takes his knowledge from people other than those from whom the first narrator of the mursal takes his, it is accepted.

Al-Jūzajānī said: When a hadith with a connected chain comes from a man who is not convincing — meaning that his narrations do not convince — and mursal reports, through routes accepted by those of discerning judgement, shore up its pillars, it is acted upon and deemed sufficient. This holds so long as it is not contradicted by a connected hadith stronger than it.
Imam Aḥmad cited this hadith as evidence, saying: The Prophet ﷺ said: “There is to be no harm and no returning of harm.”

Abū ʿAmr ibn al-Ṣalāḥ said: Al-Dāraquṭnī narrated this hadith with connected chains by several routes, and taken together they strengthen the hadith and make it good. The great majority of the people of knowledge have accepted it and used it as proof, and Abū Dāwūd's statement that it is one of the hadiths around which jurisprudence revolves suggests that it is not weak. And Allah knows best.
On the same subject there is also the hadith of Abū Ṣirmah, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: “Whoever harms, Allah will harm him; and whoever causes hardship, Allah will bring hardship upon him.”
Abū Dāwūd, al-Tirmidhī and Ibn Mājah recorded it, and al-Tirmidhī said: Good and unusual (ḥasan gharīb).
Al-Tirmidhī recorded, with a chain containing weakness, from Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: “Accursed is whoever harms a believer or schemes against him.”
His words ﷺ: “There is to be no harm and no returning of harm.”
This is the authentic narration: ḍirār, without a hamzah. It has also been narrated as iḍrār, with a hamzah; this occurs in some narrations of Ibn Mājah and al-Dāraquṭnī,
and even in some manuscripts of the Muwaṭṭaʾ. Some accepted this narration, saying that ḍarra and aḍarra are used with the same meaning. Others rejected it, saying that it has no sound basis.
They differed over whether there is any difference between the two words — I mean ḍarar and ḍirār — or not.

Some said they have a single meaning, repeated for emphasis. The well-known view is that they differ. Some then said that ḍarar is the noun and ḍirār the act; the meaning is that harm itself is negated in the Sharīʿah, and so is inflicting harm without right.
Others said: Ḍarar is to inflict harm on another by something from which one benefits oneself, and ḍirār is to inflict harm on another by something from which one gets no benefit,
like someone who withholds what does him no harm to give, while the one denied it is harmed. A group preferred this view, among them Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr and Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ.
Others said: Ḍarar is to harm someone who has not harmed you, and ḍirār is to harm someone who has harmed you, in an impermissible way.
In any case, what the Prophet ﷺ negated was only ḍarar and ḍirār without right.

As for inflicting harm on someone by right — either because he has transgressed the limits of Allah and is punished in proportion to his crime, or because he has wronged another and the wronged party seeks to answer him with justice — that is certainly not meant. What is meant is only inflicting harm without right, and this is of two kinds.
The first is where there is no aim in it other than harming that other person. There is no doubt that this is vile and unlawful.
The Qurʾān forbids causing harm in a number of places. One of them concerns bequests: Allah the Exalted says: “after any bequest that was made, or debt, without causing harm” [al-Nisāʾ 4:12].

In the hadith of Abū Hurayrah, as marfūʿ (attributed to the Prophet ﷺ): “A servant may do acts of obedience to Allah for sixty years; then death comes to him, he causes harm in his bequest, and so he enters the Fire.”

Then he recited: “These are the limits of Allah…” up to His words: “And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger and transgresses His limits, He will admit him to a Fire, abiding in it eternally” [al-Nisāʾ 4:13–14]. Al-Tirmidhī and others recorded it with this meaning.
Ibn ʿAbbās said: Causing harm in a bequest is one of the major sins. Then he recited this verse.

Causing harm in a bequest sometimes takes the form of favouring one of the heirs with more than the share Allah has fixed for him, so that the rest of the heirs are harmed by his being favoured. That is why the Prophet ﷺ said: “Allah has given everyone who has a right his right, so there is no bequest for an heir.”
Sometimes it takes the form of bequeathing more than a third to someone who is not an heir, so that the heirs' rights are reduced. That is why the Prophet ﷺ said: “A third, and a third is a lot.”
Whenever someone makes a bequest to an heir, or one of more than a third to a non-heir, his bequest is not carried out without the heirs' consent, whether or not he intended to cause harm.
If, however, he intended to cause harm by bequeathing a third to a non-heir, he sins by that intention. Is his bequest then rejected, if this is established by his own admission, or not?
Ibn ʿAṭiyyah related a reported position of Mālik that it is rejected, and it has been said that this is the analogy of Aḥmad's school.

Another concerns taking a wife back during her waiting period. The Exalted says: “Then either retain them in a fitting manner or release them in a fitting manner; and do not retain them to harm them, so that you transgress. Whoever does that has wronged himself” [al-Baqarah 2:231]. He also says:

“And their husbands have more right to take them back during that [period], if they desire reconciliation” [al-Baqarah 2:228]. This shows that whoever intends harm by taking her back sins by it. It is like what they used to do at the beginning of Islam, before divorce was limited to three: a man would divorce his wife,

leave her until her waiting period was nearly over, then take her back, then divorce her, and do so again and again without end, leaving the woman neither divorced nor kept. Allah annulled that and limited divorce to three times.

Mālik held that if a man takes his wife back before her waiting period ends and then divorces her without having touched her, then if he intended by this to harm her by lengthening the waiting period, she does not begin it afresh but builds on what has already passed of it; and if he did not intend that, she begins a new waiting period.

Some said that she builds on it in every case; this is the view of ʿAṭāʾ and Qatādah, of al-Shāfiʿī in his old opinion, and of Aḥmad in one reported position. Others said that she begins afresh in every case; this is the view of most scholars, among them Abū Qilābah, al-Zuhrī, al-Thawrī, Abū Ḥanīfah, al-Shāfiʿī in his new opinion, Aḥmad in one reported position, Isḥāq, Abū ʿUbayd and others.
Another concerns the oath of abstention (īlāʾ). When a man swears to abstain from intercourse with his wife, Allah has set a period of four months for the one who swears:
he is given a term of four months. If he returns and resumes intercourse, that is his repentance; and if he persists in abstaining, he is not allowed to go on with it.

On this there are two views among the earlier and later scholars. One is that she is divorced from him once this period has passed. The other is that he is made to stand at its end: if he returns to her, well and good; otherwise he is ordered to divorce her.

If, without any oath, he abstains from intercourse for four months with the intention of causing harm, many of the scholars of our [Ḥanbalī] school said that the ruling on him in this is that of one who has sworn the oath, and they said that this is the apparent sense of Aḥmad's words.

A number of them likewise said: If he abstains from intercourse for four months without excuse and she then asks for separation, they are separated, on the basis that in our school intercourse within this period is obligatory. They differed over whether an intention to cause harm is a condition for this or not.
The position of Mālik and his followers is that if he abstains from intercourse without excuse, his marriage is annulled, though they differ over the length of the period.

If he prolongs a journey without excuse, and his wife asks him to come back and he refuses, Mālik, Aḥmad and Isḥāq said: The judge separates them. Aḥmad set the limit at six months, and Isḥāq at the passing of two years.

Another concerns breastfeeding. The Exalted says: “No mother shall be made to suffer harm on account of her child, nor any father on account of his child” [al-Baqarah 2:233]. Mujāhid said of His words, “No mother shall be made to suffer harm on account of her child”: He is not to prevent its mother from suckling it in order to grieve her.

ʿAṭāʾ, Qatādah, al-Zuhrī, Sufyān, al-Suddī and others said: If she will accept what another woman would accept, she has more right to it. This is the explicit position of Aḥmad, even if the mother is still married to the husband.
Others said that if she is still married to him, he may prevent her from suckling it, unless it cannot be suckled by anyone else. This is the view of al-Shāfiʿī
and of some of the scholars of our school; but it is permitted only if the husband's aim in it is to keep his wife free for his own enjoyment, not merely to inflict harm on her.

His words, “nor any father on account of his child,” include the case of a divorced woman who asks to suckle her child for the wage a woman like her would receive: the father is bound to agree, whether or not someone else can be found.

This is the explicit position of Imam Aḥmad. If she asks for much more than the wage of a woman like her, and the father finds someone who will suckle the child for the standard wage, he is not bound to agree to what she asks, because she is aiming to cause harm. Imam Aḥmad stated this explicitly.

Another concerns sales: the prohibition of the sale of one in dire need (bayʿ al-muḍṭarr) has been reported. Abū Dāwūd recorded it from the hadith of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, that he addressed the people and said: A biting time will come upon people, when the well-off man will clamp his teeth on what is in his hands,

though he was not commanded to do that — Allah the Exalted says: “And do not forget graciousness among you” [al-Baqarah 2:237] — and those in dire need will be made to sell. And the Messenger of Allah ﷺ forbade the sale of one in dire need.

Al-Ismāʿīlī recorded it with the addition: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “If you have some good with which to come to your brother's aid, [then do so]; otherwise do not add ruin to his ruin.” Abū Yaʿlā al-Mawṣilī recorded something with its meaning from the hadith of Ḥudhayfah, also as marfūʿ.
ʿAbdullāh ibn Maʿqil said: A sale made out of necessity is usury (ribā).
Ḥarb said: Aḥmad was asked about the sale of one in dire need, and he disliked it. He was asked: What does it look like?
He said: He comes to you in need, and you sell him what is worth ten for twenty. Abū Ṭālib said: It was said to Aḥmad: What if he makes a profit of five on ten?
He disliked that. If the buyer is a trusting man (mustarsil) who does not know how to bargain, and the seller sells to him at a gross overcharge, that too is not permissible.
Aḥmad said: Khilābah is deception: it is to overcharge him by more than people tolerate in such dealings,
selling him what is worth a dirham for five. The position of Mālik and Aḥmad is that this gives him the option of annulling the sale.

If someone needs cash and finds no one to lend to him, so he buys a commodity for a price deferred to a set term and owed as a debt, intending to sell that commodity and take its price, there are two views on this among the Salaf. Aḥmad allowed it in one reported position, and in another said: I fear that he is someone in dire need.
If he sells the commodity back to the one who sold it to him, most of the Salaf hold that it is unlawful; this is the position of Mālik, Abū Ḥanīfah, Aḥmad and others.
Among the kinds of harm in sales is separating a mother from her child in a sale. If the child is small, it is unlawful by agreement. It has been narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said:

“Whoever separates a mother from her child, Allah will separate him from his loved ones on the Day of Resurrection.” If the mother consents to it, there is disagreement over whether it is permissible. The questions of harm in legal rulings are very many; we have mentioned these only by way of example.

The second kind is where he has some other, valid aim — such as disposing of his property in a way that serves his own interest, while this spills over into harm to another; or preventing another from benefiting from his property in order to keep it intact for himself, so that the one prevented is harmed.
As for the first — disposing of one's property in a way whose harm spills over to another — if it is done in an unusual way,

such as lighting a fire on his land on a windy day so that what lies next to it burns, he is a transgressor in doing so and is liable. If it is done in the usual way, the scholars have two well-known views on it.
One is that he is not prevented from it; this is the view of al-Shāfiʿī, Abū Ḥanīfah and others.
The second is that he is prevented; this is the view of Aḥmad, and Mālik agreed with him in some cases.

Among such cases: he opens a window in his high building overlooking his neighbour, or puts up a tall building that overlooks his neighbour without screening it; he is obliged to screen it. Aḥmad stated this explicitly, and a group of al-Shāfiʿī's followers agreed with him.

Al-Rūyānī, one of them, said in his book al-Ḥilyah: The judge uses his own judgement in this, and prevents it if he sees obstinacy and an intent to cause damage. He said: The same applies to raising a building high and blocking out the sun and the moon.

Al-Kharāʾiṭī and Ibn ʿAdī recorded with a weak chain, from ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb, from his father, from his grandfather, as marfūʿ, a long hadith on the rights of the neighbour, which includes: “Nor should he build higher than him and so block the wind from him, except with his permission.”

Another is that he digs a well near his neighbour's well so that its water drains away. It is to be filled in, according to the apparent position of the schools of Mālik and Aḥmad. Abū Dāwūd recorded in his Marāsīl, from the hadith of Abū Qilābah,
that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “Do not harm one another in digging”: that is, a man digs beside another man in order to take away his water.

Another is that he sets up on his property something that harms his neighbour's property, such as shaking, pounding and the like. He is prevented from it according to the apparent position of the schools of Mālik and Aḥmad, and that is one of the views held among the Shāfiʿīs.
The same applies if it harms the residents, such as something with a foul smell and the like.
Another is that he owns something within another man's land, and the owner of the land is harmed by his coming onto it. He is compelled to remove it, so that the harm of his entering is averted.

Abū Dāwūd recorded in his Sunan, from the hadith of Abū Jaʿfar Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī, that he related that Samurah ibn Jundab had a row of palm trees in the garden of a man of the Anṣār, who had his family living with him. Samurah used to go in to his palms,

and the man was troubled and distressed by it. He asked him to exchange them for others, and he refused. So he went to the Prophet ﷺ and told him about it. The Prophet ﷺ asked him to sell them, and he refused; he asked him to exchange them,

and he refused. He said: “Then give them to him, and you will have such-and-such” — something to make him want it — and he refused. So he said: “You are one who causes harm.” Then the Prophet ﷺ said to the Anṣārī: “Go and uproot his palms.” It has also been narrated from Abū Jaʿfar in mursal form.

Aḥmad said, in the narration of Ḥanbal, after this hadith was mentioned to him: Whatever is of this kind and involves harm, he is prevented from it; if he complies, well and good; otherwise the ruler compels him. He must not harm his brother in this, when there is benefit in it for him.
Abū Bakr al-Khallāl recorded, through the narration of ʿAbdullāh ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿAqīl, from ʿAbdullāh ibn Salīṭ ibn Qays, from his father,

that a man of the Anṣār had in his garden a palm tree belonging to another man. The owner of the palm would not keep away from it, morning and evening, and this distressed the owner of the garden. So he went to the Prophet ﷺ and told him about it.

The Prophet ﷺ said to the owner of the palm: “Take from him one of the palms next to the wall in place of your palm.” He said: No, by Allah. He said: “Then take two from me.” He said: No, by Allah. He said:
“Then give it to me.” He said: No, by Allah. The narrator said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ kept putting it to him, and he refused. So the Prophet ﷺ ordered that he be given a palm in place of his palm.
Abū Dāwūd recorded in his Marāsīl, through the narration of Ibn Isḥāq, from Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā ibn Ḥabbān, from his paternal uncle Wāsiʿ ibn Ḥabbān, who said:

Abū Lubābah had a date palm in another man's garden. The man spoke to him and said: You tread through my garden to get to your palm. I will give you one like it in your own garden, so take it out of my way. He refused him.
So he spoke to the Prophet ﷺ about it, and he said: “Abū Lubābah, take one like your palm, add it to your property, and spare your companion what he dislikes.” He said:
I will not do it. He said: “Go and bring out for him one like his palm into his garden, then put up a wall around it, for there is to be no harm and no returning of harm in Islam.”

This hadith and the one before it show that he is compelled to accept an exchange when leaving things as they are does harm to his partner or neighbour. This is like making pre-emption (shufʿah) obligatory to ward off the harm of a newly arrived partner.

It is also taken as evidence that a partner who refuses to carry out repairs is obliged to do them, and that a sale is obligatory when division is impossible. It has been narrated, from the hadith of Muḥammad ibn Abī Bakr,

from his father, as marfūʿ: “There is to be no taʿḍiyah in inheritance, except for what can bear division.” This Abū Bakr is Ibn ʿAmr ibn Ḥazm, as Imam Aḥmad said, so the hadith is mursal. Taʿḍiyah means division.

Whenever division is impossible, because the thing to be divided would be damaged by dividing it, and one of the two partners asks for it to be sold, the other is compelled and the price is divided. Aḥmad, Abū ʿUbayd and other imams stated this explicitly.
As for the second — preventing a neighbour from benefiting from one's property and making use of it — if that use harms the one whose property is being used, he may prevent it,
as when someone has a crumbling wall that cannot bear timber being laid on it. But if it does him no harm, is he obliged to allow it, so that refusing is unlawful for him, or not?
Those who said in the first case that the owner is not prevented from disposing of his property even if it harms his neighbour said here:

the neighbour may prevent others from making use of his property without his permission. Those who said there that he is prevented differed here on two views. One is that he may refuse here; this is the view of Mālik.

The second is that refusing is not permitted. This is Aḥmad's position on placing timber on a neighbour's wall; al-Shāfiʿī in his old opinion, Isḥāq, Abū Thawr, Dāwūd, Ibn al-Mundhir and ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Ḥabīb the Mālikī agreed with him, and Mālik related it from some of the judges of Madīnah.

In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Abū Hurayrah, the Prophet ﷺ said: “Let none of you prevent his neighbour from fixing a beam in his wall.” Abū Hurayrah said: Why do I see you turning away from it? By Allah, I will fling it between your shoulders.
ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb ruled against Muḥammad ibn Maslamah that he must let his neighbour's water run through his land, and said: It will pass through, even if over your belly.

On compelling this there are two reported positions of Imam Aḥmad. Abū Thawr's view is that the owner is compelled to let a neighbour's water run through his land if the neighbour runs it in a channel underground; Ḥarb al-Kirmānī transmitted this from him.

Among the things that may not be withheld, because of the harm it causes, are water and pasture. In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Abū Hurayrah, from the Prophet ﷺ: “Do not withhold surplus water in order to withhold pasture by it.”
In the Sunan of Abū Dāwūd, a man said: Prophet of Allah, what is the thing that it is not lawful to withhold?
He said: “Water.” He said: Prophet of Allah, what is the thing that it is not lawful to withhold?
He said: “Salt.” He said: What is the thing that it is not lawful to withhold? He said: “That you do good is better for you.”
It also contains that the Prophet ﷺ said: “People are partners in three things: water, fire and pasture.”
Most scholars held that the surplus of flowing water and spring water is not to be withheld in any case, whether or not the water is said to be owned by the owner of its land.

This is the view of Abū Ḥanīfah, al-Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad, Isḥāq, Abū ʿUbayd and others. Aḥmad's explicit position is that it must be given freely, without payment, for drinking, for watering animals and for watering crops; the position of Abū Ḥanīfah and al-Shāfiʿī is that it need not be given for crops.
They differed over whether it must be given in every case, or only when it is near pasture and withholding it would lead to withholding the pasture.

There are two views on this among the scholars of our school and among al-Shāfiʿī's followers, and something in Aḥmad's words indicates that the prohibition applies only to water near pasture. As for Mālik,

in his view there is no obligation to give the surplus of water that is owned through owning its source and its channel, except to someone in dire need, as with water collected in vessels; in his view the obligation applies only to the surplus of water that is not owned.
In al-Shāfiʿī's view the ruling on pasture is the same: one may withhold its surplus, except on dead land (mawāt).

The position of Abū Ḥanīfah, Aḥmad and Abū ʿUbayd is that the surplus of pasture is not to be withheld in any case. Some said: No one may withhold water and pasture except the people of the frontier posts in particular.
This is the view of al-Awzāʿī, because if the people of the frontiers lose their water and pasture, they cannot move from where they stand guarding the heartland of Islam and its people.

As for the prohibition of withholding fire, a group of jurists understood it as a prohibition of refusing someone a light taken from it, rather than the embers themselves. Some understood it as withholding the stones that strike fire,

but that is far-fetched. If it were understood as refusing the use of the fire for light, and as giving what exceeds its owner's need to someone who wants to warm himself by it or cook food on it and the like, that would not be far-fetched.

As for salt, perhaps it is to be understood as preventing people from taking it from deposits open to all; for salt is one of the surface minerals, which are not owned by bringing land into cultivation or by grant. Aḥmad stated this explicitly.
In the Sunan of Abū Dāwūd: The Prophet ﷺ granted a man a salt deposit. It was said to him: Messenger of Allah, it is like a perennial spring. So he took it back from him.
Among the things included in the general sense of his words ﷺ, “There is to be no harm,” is that Allah has never charged His servants with doing what harms them.

What He commands them is the very soundness of their religion and their worldly life, and what He forbids them is the very corruption of their religion and their worldly life; yet He has also not commanded His servants anything that harms their bodies.

That is why He dropped purification with water for the sick, saying: “Allah does not intend to place any hardship upon you” [al-Māʾidah 5:6]; He dropped fasting for the sick and the traveller, saying:

“Allah intends ease for you and does not intend hardship for you” [al-Baqarah 2:185]; and He dropped the avoidance of what iḥrām forbids, such as shaving the head and the like, for whoever is ill or has an ailment of the head, and commanded a ransom (fidyah) instead.
In the Musnad, from Ibn ʿAbbās: It was said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: Which religion is most beloved to Allah?
He said: “The upright and tolerant way (al-ḥanīfiyyah al-samḥah).”
From the hadith of ʿĀʾishah, the Prophet ﷺ said: “I have been sent with an upright and tolerant way.”
Of the same meaning is what is in the two Ṣaḥīḥs from Anas: The Prophet ﷺ saw a man walking, and it was said
that he had vowed to go on Ḥajj on foot. He said: “Allah has no need of his walking; let him ride.” In one narration: “Allah has no need of this man tormenting himself.”
In the Sunan, from ʿUqbah ibn ʿĀmir: His sister vowed to walk to the House, and the Prophet ﷺ said: “Allah does nothing with your sister's hardship; let her ride.”

Scholars have differed over the ruling on someone who vows to perform Ḥajj on foot. Some said that he is not bound to walk and may ride in any case; this is a reported position of Aḥmad, and of al-Awzāʿī.

Aḥmad said: He fasts three days. Al-Awzāʿī said: He owes the expiation for an oath. The well-known view is that he is bound to walk if he is able. If he is unable, some said that he rides when he can no longer walk and owes nothing; this is one of al-Shāfiʿī's two views.
Others said that he also owes the expiation for an oath; this is the view of al-Thawrī, and of Aḥmad in one reported position.
Others said that he owes a blood sacrifice; a group of the Salaf said this, among them ʿAṭāʾ, Mujāhid, al-Ḥasan, al-Layth, and Aḥmad in one reported position.

Others said that he gives in charity what it would have cost to hire his mount. This is narrated from al-Awzāʿī, who related it from ʿAṭāʾ; and it is narrated from ʿAṭāʾ that he gives in charity the amount of his expenses at the House.

A group of the Companions and others said: Riding does not discharge it; rather he performs Ḥajj the following year, walking the stretches he rode and riding the stretches he walked. Some added: And he owes a sacrificial animal (hady). This is Mālik's view when what he rode was a great deal.

Also included in its general sense is that someone in debt is not to be pressed for payment while he is in hardship; rather he is given time until he is in ease. The Exalted says: “And if [the debtor] is in hardship, then [let there be] respite until ease” [al-Baqarah 2:280]. The great majority of scholars hold this, contrary to Shurayḥ, who said

that the verse applies only to the usurious debts of the Jāhiliyyah; the majority went by the general wording. Nor is the debtor required to pay his debt from things whose leaving his ownership would harm him,
such as his clothes and the dwelling he needs, and likewise his servant, nor from what he needs to trade with to support himself and his dependants. This is the position of Imam Aḥmad.
